blocks.text: The chapter presents Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem as opponents whose interests were affected by Jerusalem’s fortification. Their repeated invitations, accusations, and intimidation are part of the narrative’s account of pressure against the rebuilding work. This portrayal should not be turned into a timeless ethnic conflict or used to vilify modern neighboring peoples.

The wall’s completion on Elul 25, after fifty-two days, forms the chapter’s answer to the campaign of opposition. The narrative says that surrounding nations recognized the work as accomplished with God’s help; its point is not merely that construction succeeded, but that the outcome changed how the opponents understood it.

Nehemiah 6 belongs to an extended first-person memoir that gives vivid testimony about court life, rebuilding, prayer, opposition, and reform. The book as a whole also includes third-person narrative, lists, material about Ezra, and editorial transitions, so it should not be read as either straightforward autobiography throughout or as wholly fictionalized.
